title: A thousand days
hook: day one thousand on the hill: a moment to be glad you came this far

segments.voice: Yesterday, sant-sipahi, and your line was they served again. Did you ask an older person what they remember? Today the story pauses, because of the number on the bell. Day one thousand.

The hill doesn't hand out trophies. There's no holy day on any calendar for this one, just a count of mornings and evenings when you opened this and listened. But before the story turns toward a very hard year, which it does tomorrow, it's worth stopping on the path, turning around, and looking back down at the first step, far below. So today there's no battle and no reform campaign. There's the place you started, and the place you're standing.
screen: `DAY ONE THOUSAND.` → `STOP ON THE PATH.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE HILL.`

segments.voice: First, where you began. Day one on this path was a kitchen in Amritsar that feeds everyone who walks in, for free, and the word was seva, selfless service. Your line that day was one quiet thing for someone. Second, the next step. Day two was Waheguru, the word Sikhs say for God, and the line was simply wow: wonder before the One. Everything since has been built on those two. Gurus and their hymns, martyrs and builders, soldiers and reformers, and a free kitchen that kept feeding strangers all the way through. Third, the spirit for the road. Sikhs have a phrase for the mood they hope to carry through good years and terrible ones: chardi kala. It means rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart. It isn't pretending things are fine. It's staying turned toward the light when they're not. The Ardas, the standing prayer you met three days ago in a trench, closes by asking that through Nanak the Name may bring rising spirits, and that by God's will all may be well. Chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, side by side. Fourth, the next stretch. The story is about to go through the year of Partition, and it won't be easy to hear. Chardi kala is not a way of skipping the hard chapters. It's how Sikhs have walked through them. That's today's line: a thousand days. Not a finish line. A place to stand for a moment, glad, before the path goes on.
screen: `DAY ONE: SEVA, A KITCHEN IN AMRITSAR.` · `DAY TWO: WAHEGURU, WOW.` · `CHARDI KALA: RISING SPIRITS.` · `NOT A WAY AROUND THE HARD PARTS.` · then, large: `A THOUSAND DAYS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes looking back. Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Go back to where you were when you began this path: the room, the season, what was on your mind then. Don't judge that person. Just look at them kindly. Then come back to this room, and notice one thing that's different now, however small: a word you know, a habit you kept, a story you could tell someone tonight. Breathe in on then. Breathe out on now. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Chardi kala, rising spirits, an upward-climbing heart: a long count of ordinary mornings on the path, from seva and Waheguru to here. Today's word.
Your line: a place to stand, glad. Today, do one quiet thing for someone, the way day one asked, and notice that you still can. Day one thousand.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits, as the outlook to keep in good times and hard ones, and the Ardas said at the close of worship ends by asking for chardi kala and the good of all.
